clinicalPearls: Typically affects multiparous premenopausal women who describe a dull, aching chronic pelvic pain lasting more than six months
The pain characteristically worsens towards the end of the day, on prolonged standing, and after intercourse, and eases on lying down
Deep dyspareunia and a post-coital ache are common, and varicosities may be visible over the vulva, buttocks, or upper thighs
Dilated, tortuous, incompetent ovarian and pelvic veins underlie the syndrome and can be demonstrated on Doppler imaging
It is a diagnosis of exclusion; other causes of chronic pelvic pain must be considered before symptoms are attributed to venous congestion
Ovarian and pelvic vein embolisation is the mainstay of definitive treatment, offering symptom relief in a majority of appropriately selected women
Secondary causes of pelvic venous obstruction, such as left renal vein or iliac vein compression, should be sought before treatment
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome results from incompetence and dilatation of the ovarian and internal iliac venous tributaries. Failure of the venous valves permits retrograde flow and pooling of blood within the pelvic veins, producing chronic venous congestion. Oestrogen has a venodilatory effect and, together with the increased pelvic venous capacity acquired during pregnancy, contributes to the tendency of the condition to occur in premenopausal parous women. The engorged veins and associated stasis are thought to generate the characteristic positional pelvic pain.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic pelvic inflammatory disease and adhesions
Interstitial cystitis or bladder pain syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound with Doppler to identify dilated pelvic veins and demonstrate reflux
Transabdominal and transvaginal duplex assessment of ovarian vein diameter and flow direction
Magnetic resonance venography or CT venography to map the pelvic venous anatomy
Catheter venography, regarded as the reference standard, which also allows treatment at the same sitting
Investigations to exclude other pelvic pathology, including laparoscopy where indicated
redFlags: Features suggesting an underlying secondary obstruction such as nutcracker or May-Thurner physiology
A pelvic or renal mass causing venous compression
Haematuria or flank pain pointing to left renal vein compression
New or atypical symptoms that raise concern for malignancy
reference.prognosis: Many women obtain durable relief of pain following ovarian vein embolisation, although symptoms may persist or recur, particularly if an underlying obstructive cause has not been addressed.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosis, since pelvic varices are common and frequently asymptomatic incidental findings
Failing to exclude a secondary obstructive cause such as renal or iliac vein compression
Attributing all chronic pelvic pain to congestion without excluding coexisting pathology
Offering intervention without correlating imaging findings with the clinical picture
management: Offer ovarian and pelvic vein embolisation as the definitive treatment, occluding the incompetent refluxing veins
Trial hormonal venoconstriction with progestogens such as medroxyprogesterone or a GnRH analogue to reduce venous congestion and pain
Provide analgesia for the chronic positional pelvic pain
Exclude other causes of chronic pelvic pain before attributing symptoms to venous congestion, using laparoscopy where indicated
Identify and treat an underlying obstructive cause such as nutcracker or May-Thurner compression with venous stenting to prevent persistence or recurrence
Refer to interventional radiology, reserving surgical vein ligation or hysterectomy for selected refractory cases
